note: Synthesised from per-letter recipes, not recorded.

ancient.note: Fifth-century Athens, following the reconstruction this hall’s alphabet already states. The ancient accent was melodic — a rise in pitch, not a beat of loudness — and these clips render it as stress. That is a trade rather than a hard limit: the one synthesis mode available that accepts a pitch contour speaks only American English sounds, so buying the accent would cost the trill, the geminates, the front rounded vowel and every unaspirated stop. And the reconstruction is itself an argument, not a recording.

0.why: Both alphas are short open [a], the λ is clear (non-velarised) as in Greek, the stress is on the first syllable, and there is no vowel reduction anywhere — Italian gives all four for free in one word-shaped token (verified read as a word, 0.599 s at default rate). The φ is deliberately spelled p, not f: in the fifth century φ was still an aspirated stop [pʰ], so an unaspirated [p] misses by one laryngeal feature, while the [f] of Italian 'alfa' or Greek άλφα misses by a whole manner of articulation and is four centuries too young.
0.compromise: The aspiration is simply absent: you hear [ˈalpa], not [ˈalpʰa]. This is a real loss, but a smaller one than it looks, and the two English proposals for this letter were worse. English aspirates strongly only in the onset of a STRESSED syllable, and this φ sits in an unstressed one — so 'al-pah' or 'arl pah' on Daniel buys a weak aspirate and pays for it with a dark [ɫ], a long back [ɑː] for both alphas, and a mid-word pause that moves the prominence onto the second syllable, inverting the accent of ἄλφα. To hear what this φ should sound like, click Phi, where the aspirate is word-initial and stressed. Also: this will not sound like English 'AL-fa', which is the point, but the page should say so or it reads as a bug. The accent is stress, not the Attic pitch rise.

1.why: A real Italian word, so it comes from Luca's lexicon rather than from letter-to-sound guessing. Italian 'beta' is [ˈbɛta]: a true voiced stop [b] where Modern Greek β is now [v]; the open [ɛ] that η needs rather than the close [e] of ε; an unaspirated dental [t] for τ, where an English voice would aspirate it and an American one would flap it to [ɾ]; and a pure unreduced final [a]. Italian lengthens a stressed vowel in a non-final open syllable, so the η comes out genuinely long.
1.compromise: The open quality here is Luca's lexical entry, and it cannot be steered: `say -v Luca "bèta"` produces a byte-identical file to "beta" (a77a707f98463b4915227388b778e04c), so the grave accent does nothing. If his entry were close-mid [e] there would be no way to correct it and no way for us to hear that it had gone wrong — Italian dictionaries give [ˈbɛta], which is why confidence is medium rather than high. The vowel length is allophonic (a by-product of Italian stress in an open syllable), not phonemic as it was in Attic. βῆτα carried a circumflex — a rise-then-fall in pitch across the long η — and Luca gives loudness and duration instead.

2.why: γάμμα is one of four names in this alphabet built on a doubled consonant, and Italian is the only available language with phonemic gemination — 'gamma' is a real Italian word, [ˈɡamma], with a genuinely held [mː] across the syllable boundary. It also gives a plain voiced stop [ɡ] with no digraph and therefore no prenasalisation risk, where Melina's bare γ before α would be the fricative [ɣ] and her digraph γκ would import a nasal. Both alphas are short and pure.
2.compromise: Essentially nothing is lost segmentally; this is among the closest recipes in the set. The one correction to make on the page is that Modern Greek's lack of geminates is NOT a hard limit of the toolkit, as one scheme claimed — it is a limit of the Greek voice only, and Italian recovers the doubled consonant here, at Kappa and at Koppa. The acute on γάμμα was a pitch rise; Luca gives stress.

3.why: A real Spanish word, [ˈdelta], and Spanish supplies the one thing Italian cannot here: a close-mid [e]. Allen reconstructs classical ε as close-mid [e], contrasting with η's open [ɛː] — Italian 'delta' gives [ˈdɛlta], which collapses ε into η's quality and leaves the pair distinguished by length alone. Everything else is also right in Spanish: phrase-initial /d/ is a true stop, /t/ is unaspirated dental, /l/ is clear, and Spanish reduces no vowel, so the final [a] is full.
3.compromise: This follows Allen against the site's own gloss, which calls ε 'short e as in pet' — that gloss describes [ɛ], and what you will hear is closer to the vowel of Spanish 'de'. If the site prefers its own gloss, Luca 'delta' gives [ˈdɛlta] instead; but then Delta, Epsilon, Eta, Beta, Zeta and Theta all carry one and the same vowel and the ε/η contrast disappears from the audio entirely. Spanish /e/ before a coda /l/ is somewhat lowered, so the realisation sits a little below a cardinal [e] — between the two targets rather than squarely on Allen's. Voice differs from the Italian majority; Jorge is used for exactly the three names built on short ε or ο. The acute on δέλτα was a pitch rise, rendered as stress.

4.why: 'Épsilon' is the standard Spanish spelling of the letter name and the written acute is obligatory Spanish orthography in that position, so it is honoured rather than stripped — verified: 'épsilon' (0.858 s, 6fb63063…), 'epsilon' (0.828 s, 2e66da47…) and 'epsilón' (0.783 s, b272467c…) are three different files. That puts the prominence on the letter's OWN vowel, which is what the reader has clicked to hear, and Spanish gives it as a clean close-mid [e] — Allen's ε. Spanish also keeps the [ps] cluster, does not aspirate the p, and reduces none of the following vowels to schwa the way English would.
4.compromise: The name is a Byzantine coinage, not a classical one: a fifth-century Athenian called this letter simply εἶ, a bare long [eː]. 'Ἒ ψιλόν' ('plain e') was invented to distinguish it from the by-then-homophonous αι. I use it because the site displays 'Epsilon'. Two further mismatches. The historical phrase was oxytone — the accent belonged on -λόν — whereas this recipe stresses the first syllable; that is the modern convention and it is chosen deliberately, so that the vowel the letter stands for is the loud one. And as at Delta, the close-mid [e] follows Allen rather than the site's 'pet' gloss. Accent is stress, not pitch.

5.why: Italian voices /s/ before a voiced consonant without exception ('sdraiare' [zdraˈjaːre]), so orthographic word-initial 'sd' is realised [zd] by rule — the cluster that is the whole point of this letter, and one no other installed language can spell. The grave is live in this position: 'sdèta' (0.663 s, 50ae3eab…) differs from 'sdeta' (0.644 s, c8ad951d…), so the vowel is biased to the open [ɛː] of ζῆτα rather than left to a nonce default. The τ is Italian, hence unaspirated; the final [a] is unreduced.
5.compromise: Three honest caveats. (a) [zd] versus [dz] is genuinely contested. Allen argues [zd] and the site follows him; this recipe silently takes his side. (b) If Luca's s-voicing is implemented lexically rather than phonologically, the output is [ˈsdɛta] — and that is not a near-miss, it is a voiceless-plus-voiced cluster no reconstruction proposes. Alice (it_IT) reads the same string and could be used as a second opinion by anyone able to listen. (c) Do not believe the byte-size arguments the schemes offered for the Greek alternative ζντέτα: file duration cannot distinguish [zd] from [znd], and that spelling's behaviour is undocumented — it was not risked. The circumflex is rendered as stress.

6.why: The whole name is the letter's own value plus -ta, so the vowel carries everything, and Italian is the only voice that delivers it. The grave demonstrably fires here — 'èta' (0.599 s, 4ea25498…) against 'eta' (0.519 s, 1e9d5057…), an 80 ms difference consistent with the open-vowel lengthening Italian applies to a stressed non-final open syllable — so this is a genuinely long open [ɛː], the 'air' vowel the site glosses, produced natively rather than simulated by tempo. Unaspirated [t], full final [a].
6.compromise: Italian vowel length is allophonic — the [ɛː] is long because it is stressed and open, not because the phonology distinguishes long from short — so the quantity that was phonemic in Attic is here an accident of Italian. This letter is the one where every scheme was tempted by voice consistency and got it wrong: Melina fed 'έτα' says [ˈeta], which is the ancient value of EPSILON, so the single contrast this letter exists to teach would have been inverted. ἦτα carried a circumflex, a rise-then-fall within the long vowel; that is flattened to stress, and on a name this short the accent is nearly the whole prosody.

7.why: Theta is an aspirated stop [tʰ], not the English fricative [θ], and English word-initial /t/ is a real [tʰ] with a 60–80 ms voice-onset delay — the only source of one on this machine. The spelling avoids 'th' for exactly that reason. Daniel rather than an American voice on two counts: he is non-rhotic, so 'air' is a monophthongal long [ɛː] and precisely the site's own gloss for η; and he does not flap intervocalic /t/, which would turn the medial τ into [ɾ]. Written as one word so the second t stays inside an unstressed onset.
7.compromise: Three real losses, and one risk. The final α reduces: 'tairta', 'tairtah' and 'tairtar' all produce the identical file (32b403d9…), so no spelling recovers a full short [a] — the word ends in a reduced or long back English vowel, and Attic had no vowel reduction. The medial τ is weakly aspirated rather than plain: English aspirates unstressed onsets too, just less, so the θ/τ contrast inside this one name is compressed, not preserved. The voice is audibly a different speaker from most of the alphabet — worth telling the reader that this is the one place where an English voice is more accurate than a Greek or Italian one. The risk: if Daniel's SQUARE vowel is the conservative centring diphthong [ɛə] rather than modern monophthongal [ɛː], eta arrives as a diphthong; duration testing cannot tell the two apart. Circumflex rendered as stress.

8.why: ἰῶτα is three syllables with a genuine hiatus, and every language here wants to crush the initial ι into a glide — Melina fed 'ιώτα' produces [ˈʝota], the modern Greek name, two syllables with a palatal onset and the stress on the wrong syllable, which is exactly the confusion this page exists to dispel. The space forces the issue: 'i' is a real Italian word (the plural article, [i]) and gets its own syllable by construction rather than by hope. 'òta' then supplies the open [ɔː] of the circumflexed ω — and the grave is live here, 'òta' (0.619 s, 5a776744…) against 'ota' (0.524 s, 16d9c4b5…). Phrase stress falls on the second word, matching ἰῶτα. Unaspirated τ and a full final [a] come free.
8.compromise: The word boundary leaves a slight juncture where Greek had smooth hiatus — the price of guaranteeing the syllable that the letter is named for. The German alternative (Anna 'Iota') was rejected: German glides prevocalic i readily (Nation, Familie) and German's own dictionary form of this word is Jota [ˈjoːta], so it is a coin-flip, and it would give a close [oː] where ω was open. The ω's length here comes from Italian stressed-open-syllable lengthening, not from phonemic quantity. The circumflex on ω was a rise-then-fall within one long vowel — the most conspicuously untranslatable accent in the system, since stress cannot express a contour on a single syllable at all.

9.why: Two things must be right and Italian is the only voice that gives both. The κ must be UNASPIRATED — the site's own gloss is 'k as in skill' — and an English voice would say [kʰ], which is Chi, not Kappa. And κάππα has a true geminate [pː] with a real held closure, which only Italian can produce. 'Cappa' is an everyday Italian word (cape, hood), so it is lexical rather than guessed; the c-spelling removes any doubt about the letter-to-sound rule. Both alphas are short and pure, the final one unreduced.
9.compromise: Nothing material is lost segmentally — this is one of the two or three most accurate recipes here. Note for the reader that the deliberate contrast is Kappa (Italian, unaspirated) against Chi (Daniel, aspirated), and that this is a cross-speaker comparison: different language, different sex, different vocal tract. The only thing to listen for is the burst at the very start; everything after it is noise for this purpose. Modern Greek would have given [ˈkapa] — correct but degeminated. The acute is rendered as stress, not as the pitch rise it was.

10.why: The awkward part is the medial -μβδ- cluster, and 'lambda' is a real Italian word that keeps it intact as [ˈlambda] with two true voiced stops. Modern Greek has no spelling for [mbd] at all: λάμβδα gives [ˈlamvða] and λάμδα gives [ˈlamða], fricativising both stops, while λάμπντα is a gamble on cluster parsing that nobody in this loop can hear. Italian /l/ is clear and dental like the Greek, where English would give a dark [ɫ]; both [a]s are short and pure, and the final one is not reduced to schwa.
10.compromise: The [b] sits between a nasal and a stop and may be very short, close to a transitional closure. The older and possibly original form of the name is λάβδα, without the nasal — both are attested, and this recipe takes the fuller one. A voice change away from Greek is unavoidable here, but it costs nothing, since the Greek alternatives all lose a stop. The acute is rendered as stress.

11.why: This name is nothing but [m] plus the front rounded vowel [yː], and [y] is the one ancient vowel Modern Greek definitively cannot make — υ became [i] centuries ago, so Melina's 'μι' would be [mi], the modern name and the wrong vowel. 'My' is the German dictionary name of this very letter, [myː], so the vowel is lexical and genuinely long rather than guessed: German lengthens a stressed vowel in an open syllable, and this is one. Verified as a single syllable (0.479 s at default rate). Rate 140 because this monosyllable's nucleus is long and there is no short monosyllabic name anywhere in the alphabet for the slower tempo to mislead against.
11.compromise: The voice is German and the timbre changes. Do not credit the lengthening-h device that two schemes used here: `say -v Anna "Müh"` is byte-identical to "Mü" (4f8925bf…), so the h is stripped before letter-to-sound and contributes nothing — the length comes from the open stressed syllable, which is why the recipe must keep the syllable open. Beyond that this is very close: German [yː] is tense and peripheral, the same vowel as reconstructed Attic ὖ. μῦ carried a circumflex, a rise-and-fall across that long vowel, and Anna gives a flat stressed vowel; on a monosyllable the accent is the entire prosody, so this is the letter where the loss of pitch is most total. The classical name μῦ survived unchanged into the Byzantine list, so label and audio agree here.

12.why: Identical logic to Mu, and deliberately the same voice and rate so the two form an audible minimal pair, [myː] against [nyː] — which is exactly what a learner needs, and exactly what μῦ and νῦ are in Greek. 'Ny' is the German dictionary name of ν, [nyː], so the long tense front rounded vowel is lexical rather than a nonce reading. German /n/ is alveolar, as Greek ν was. Verified as a single syllable (0.464 s at default rate).
12.compromise: Voice changes to German. Again, the length is German open-syllable lengthening, not a spelling trick: 'Nüh' and 'Nü' are byte-identical (56d671a6…), so the lengthening-h one scheme relied on does nothing, and the claim offered as proof that it worked — that Nüh and Müh had matching durations — was not true (0.464 s against 0.474 s) and would have proved nothing about the vowel had it been. The circumflex of νῦ is flattened to stress, with nothing else in the monosyllable to carry the accent. The name νῦ is classical and matches the displayed label.

13.why: German ⟨x⟩ is [ks] by native rule (Hexe, Nixe, Xylophon), 'Xi' is the German name of the letter, and a stop inside an initial [ks] cluster carries no aspiration — so the k is both present and breathless, which an English voice would ruin ('xi' in English is [zaɪ] or [saɪ]). German also lengthens the stressed vowel in this open syllable, giving a real [iː] that no Greek voice can. Verified read as a word, 0.549 s at default rate; note that Anna 'Ksi' runs 0.953 s and is evidently not being read as one.
13.compromise: The name is late. The classical fifth-century name was ξεῖ with a long close [eː]; the [iː] form is Hellenistic and later, so the audio matches the site's 'Xi' label rather than what a contemporary of Sophocles said — the same is true of Pi, Phi, Chi and Psi. Melina's native ξι was rejected because Modern Greek palatalises velars before front vowels, and importing a living modern allophone into a reconstruction is the specific failure this page exists to avoid; the German cluster is not palatalised. Voice changes to German, matching Psi so the two cluster-letters form a pair. Circumflex rendered as stress.

14.why: 'Ómicron' is the standard Spanish form and the acute is obligatory orthography there, so it is honoured — verified: 'ómicron' (0.798 s, a79e76ff…), 'omicron' (0.783 s, 46c9f4dc…) and 'omicrón' (0.763 s, c974c1ef…) are three distinct files. That stresses the letter's own vowel, and Spanish gives it as a single stable close-mid [o] — Allen's ο, and crucially NOT the open [ɔː] of omega, so the pair contrast survives as quality and not merely as tempo. Spanish also gives an unaspirated [k], a tap in the -cr- cluster (much closer to Greek ρ than any English r), and no vowel reduction anywhere.
14.compromise: This follows Allen against the site's own gloss, which calls ο 'short o as in German Gott', i.e. the open [ɔ]. Italian would give that open vowel — Luca's 'omicron' is [ˈɔmikron] — but then Omicron and Omega share a quality and only length distinguishes them, and Italian cannot be steered to a close [o] in a stressed syllable ('ómicron' is byte-identical to 'omicron' in Luca's voice). Note the resulting inconsistency inside this set: Koppa, whose ο is the same phoneme, is voiced by Luca 'coppa' with an open [ɔ], because there the geminate was worth more. The truth is that Allen's ο sat between the two and no single voice here can hold the line everywhere. The name is Byzantine: classically the letter was just οὖ, a bare long close [oː], and the phrase ὂ μικρόν was oxytone where this recipe stresses the first syllable. Accent is stress, not pitch.

15.why: The entire content of this recipe is the ABSENCE of aspiration. Italian initial /p/ is a plain [p] — the p of 'spin', which is what Attic π was — where any English voice says [pʰiː] and turns Pi into Phi, destroying the single most important contrast in the Greek stop system. Italian also gives a tense undiphthongised [i], lengthened by stress in this open syllable, where English [iː] glides. Verified read as a word (0.429 s at default rate). Rate 140 as for the other long-nucleus monosyllables.
15.compromise: This letter and Phi are the cleanest demonstration of the whole method — the same vowel, one voice chosen against aspiration and one chosen for it — but they are two different speakers, a male Italian against a male Englishman, and that must be said: the only thing to compare is the first 60 ms. The name is post-classical (πεῖ [peː] in the fifth century, πῖ later), used to match the displayed label. Vowel length here is Italian's allophonic lengthening plus the slow rate, not phonemic quantity. Circumflex rendered as stress.

16.why: Italian word-initial ⟨r⟩ is a multi-contact trill, the site's 'trilled r', where Modern Greek ρ is normally a single tap and every English r is an approximant that is not a rhotic trill in any useful sense. And Italian has a live phonological rule that the schemes missed while arguing about the accent mark: a word-final STRESSED ⟨o⟩ is always open [ɔ] (però, andò, no), so the vowel should come out with omega's quality without needing any diacritic — which is just as well, since 'rho', 'ro' and 'rò' all produce one identical file (d2c07b49…). 'Rho' is also a real Italian word (the letter, and the town outside Milan), so the token is lexical.
16.compromise: The weakest letter in the set, and it fails on two of three features. (1) The rough breathing is gone, and it is the interesting part: initial ῥ was voiceless, [r̥] — a whispered trill, which is why Latin wrote it 'rh' and why the site notes 'breathy rh at word-start'. No voice on this machine can devoice a trill on demand, so you will hear a fully voiced [r]. (2) The vowel is short. Italian lengthens stressed vowels in NON-final open syllables only; word-final stressed vowels are short (città, così), which is the one position where Italian cannot help — the slow rate adds absolute duration but no phonemic length, and the open quality, though predicted by rule, is not verifiable here. (3) A TTS trill may surface as a single tap. Marked low for that reason, not because a better option was passed over: Jorge's 'ro' guarantees a Spanish trill but gives a close-mid [o], which would make ῥῶ rhyme with ὂ μικρόν — a worse error than an uncertain aperture. Circumflex rendered as stress.

17.why: A real Italian word, [ˈsiɡma]: initial /s/ before a vowel is unambiguously voiceless (the s-voicing rule that gives Zeta its [zd] fires only before a voiced consonant, so it does not apply here), and Italian reads medial 'gm' as a true stop-plus-nasal, as in 'dogma'. Melina is specifically wrong here — Greek γ before μ is the voiced fricative [ɣ], giving [ˈsiɣma] — and the digraph fix, σίγκμα, asks a Greek voice for /ŋɡm/, a three-consonant sequence that occurs in no Greek word and would most likely arrive with an intrusive nasal.
17.compromise: Almost nothing is lost, and one apology the other schemes offered should be struck: the usual lexical form of the name is σίγμα, paroxytone with a SHORT iota, so there is no long vowel here to fail to reproduce, and no rate compensation is warranted. (Some texts write σῖγμα; if that accentuation is preferred, the length is indeed absent, because Italian shortens a stressed vowel in a closed syllable and no `-r` setting can restore a within-word quantity contrast.) The voice is Italian rather than Greek. The accent is stress, not the pitch rise.

18.why: Two requirements, both met by a real Italian word. The τ must be UNASPIRATED — the site's gloss is 't as in stop' — and Italian gives that natively where an English voice would aspirate it into a theta. And the name needs a true falling diphthong [au̯] in one syllable, which Italian still has as a live phoneme sequence (auto, aura, causa) with an unambiguously open [a] first element. The Greek respelling route fails here: Modern Greek αυ is [af]/[av], so 'ταυ' would give [taf], and the workaround 'τάου' asks a language with no /au̯/ diphthong left to make two vowels behave as one.
18.compromise: The Italian offglide may be a shade more consonantal than the Greek second mora was. The circumflex sat across the diphthong as a rise-then-fall over its two morae; Italian renders it as stress on the first element, so the internal shape of the accent is lost even though the syllable is right. Rate 140 because the nucleus is bimoraic. Otherwise this is one of the most faithful recipes in the set — Jorge's Spanish 'tau' would serve equally well and is the fallback if Luca's diphthong disappoints.

19.why: 'Ypsilon' is the actual German word for this letter — the Duden headword, [ˈʏpsilɔn] — so it comes from the lexicon with no letter-to-sound gamble. (Note that 'Üpsilon' is NOT German, and Anna reads the two differently: 0.933 s against 0.828 s.) German ⟨y⟩ here is the front rounded vowel, the ancient value of υ and the entire reason this letter is interesting; Melina would give [ˈipsilon], unrounding it to the modern value and erasing the letter's point. German also keeps the [ps] cluster with no aspiration on the p, and ends in a clean oral [ɔn], where French would risk nasalising it to [-lɔ̃]. Same voice as Mu and Nu so the three [y] letters are directly comparable.
19.compromise: The rounding, which is the feature that matters, is right; the length and tenseness are not. German ⟨y⟩ before a consonant cluster is the SHORT LAX [ʏ], slightly lower and more centralised, where the ancient ὖ was a long tense [yː] — and no spelling recovers it, since Anna strips the lengthening h ('Ühpsilon' is byte-identical to 'Üpsilon', dbc50a2b…). To hear the tense long version of this same vowel, click Mu or Nu, where it is lexical. German stresses the first syllable, whereas the Byzantine phrase ὖ ψιλόν was oxytone. And the name is itself Byzantine: classically the letter was just ὖ — usefully, that is approximately the first syllable of what you hear. Accent is stress, not pitch.

20.why: Phi was an aspirated STOP [pʰ], not the fricative [f] it became in Roman times, and English word-initial /p/ is a genuine [pʰ] — the only source of one here. 'Pea' is a real English word, so the output is lexically guaranteed [pʰiː], which is the reconstructed name almost exactly, and the spelling crucially avoids 'ph', which would trigger [f] in every language on this machine. Leaving the Greek voice is not a compromise here but a correction: Melina's 'φι' would give [fi], a labiodental fricative four centuries too young.
20.compromise: Voice changes to British English. The vowel is English FLEECE, slightly diphthongised toward [ɪi], where Greek [iː] was a steady monophthong. English initial aspiration is probably heavier than the Attic was — ancient φ was an aspirated stop, not the strongly puffed English onset. The name is post-classical: φεῖ [pʰeː] in the fifth century, φῖ later. Use it as a deliberate pair with Pi — same vowel, one with the breath and one without — but be aware that the pair crosses two speakers and two languages, so only the onset is comparable. Listeners who know the letter as 'fie' will find this startling, which is the point and should be said on the page. Circumflex rendered as stress.

21.why: 'Key' is [kʰiː] in any English variety — a real word, a real aspirated velar stop, and the reconstructed name essentially unaltered. No other voice can approach it: Modern Greek χ before a front vowel is [ç], a palatal fricative, a completely different segment from the classical aspirated stop; Italian 'chi' is [ki], which is Kappa, not Chi; German 'Ki' would also aspirate but adds a fifth-voice inconsistency for no gain. Same voice as Theta and Phi so the three aspirates form a set the ear can group, and the same rate as Kappa's Italian counterpart is deliberately NOT used — see the compromise.
21.compromise: Voice changes to British English, and slight English diphthongisation of the [iː]. The name is post-classical (χεῖ [kʰeː] originally). The pairing to make on the page is Kappa (Luca, unaspirated) against Chi (Daniel, aspirated) — the same stop with and without the breath, which is the distinction the whole reconstruction hangs on and which Modern Greek and Erasmian pronunciation obliterate in opposite directions. But that pair crosses speakers, languages and tempo (Kappa runs at 160 as a polysyllable, Chi at 140 as a long monosyllable), so the reader must be told to listen to the burst at the start and ignore everything else. Circumflex rendered as stress.

22.why: Word-initial [ps] is something English structurally cannot do — an English voice reading 'psi' says [saɪ], dropping the p entirely. German keeps it (Psychologie, Psalm), 'Psi' is the German name of the letter, and a stop at the head of an initial cluster is not aspirated, so the p is plain as ψ = π+σ requires. German also lengthens the stressed vowel in this open syllable, giving a real [iː]. Paired with Xi in the same voice, since ξ and ψ are the matched stop-plus-sigma pair. Verified read as a word, 0.499 s at default rate.
22.compromise: Melina's native 'ψι' was the obvious choice and I rejected it on evidence: it runs 0.898 s against 0.539 s for 'πι' and 0.614 s for 'ξι', and close to the 1.018 s of the isolated letter 'ψ' — a monosyllable taking half again as long as its neighbours is the signature of a token not being read as a word. (Melina 'ψει', the classical spelling, behaves normally at 0.604 s and is the Greek fallback if one is wanted.) Voice changes to German. The name is the later form: classically ψεῖ with [eː], shifted to [iː] in the Hellenistic period, so the audio matches the site's label rather than the fifth century. Circumflex rendered as stress.

23.why: Written as the two words it historically was, ὦ μέγα ('big o'), which solves the problem that defeated every one-word attempt. Italian's own stress in 'omega' falls on -me-, so the letter's own vowel arrives short and unstressed, and the accent mark cannot move it: 'òmega' differs from 'omega' by 15 ms and 'omèga' is byte-identical to it. Split into two words, the ὦ is its own phrase-initial stressed word and gets Italian's open [ɔ] with real prominence and phrase lengthening, while 'mega' keeps its native stress — which is where μέγα's accent belongs anyway. Verified as two words (0.698 s, 6569e5c9…). The γ is a true stop [ɡ] with no digraph, avoiding the prenasalisation that Greek γκ carries word-internally.
23.compromise: The word boundary inserts a small pause the site's one-word label does not imply. The long open [ɔː] is Italian's phrase-level lengthening plus prominence, not phonemic quantity. The [ɛ] of Italian 'mega' is more open than the short close [e] of μέγα — a minor error inside a syllable that is not the letter. The name is Byzantine; classically the letter was just ὦ, a bare long [ɔː], which is exactly the first word of this recording, so a reader wanting the classical name can be told to listen only to the start. Clicking Omicron and Omega in succession will not give a clean minimal pair, because they are two different speakers of two different languages — what it does give is the real quality difference, close [o] against open [ɔː], which one voice alone could not produce. The circumflex was a rise-then-fall on that long vowel; here it is loudness and duration.

24.why: A real Italian word, and segmentally it needs exactly what Italian provides and Greek cannot: a true stop [d] (Melina's δ is [ð]), a true stop [ɡ] (her γ before α is [ɣ]), and the geminate [mː]. The Greek respelling route, ντίγκαμα, needs two digraphs, of which the medial γκ is prenasalised [ŋɡ] in standard Modern Greek as the norm — real-word probes put the added nasal at 105–110 ms — so it would deliver [ˈdiŋɡama], with the geminate lost as well.
24.compromise: Two things, and the second is the more interesting. (1) The stress is wrong: Italian words in -amma are paroxytone, so this comes out [diˈɡamma] where δίγαμμα is proparoxytone, [ˈdiɡamma]. Italian orthography cannot move it — 'dìgamma' returns a different waveform at exactly the same duration (0.793 s both), which is a perturbation, not a relocation, and 'di gamma' as two words was no better. (2) This is the only letter whose audio contains no trace of the sound it stands for. 'Digamma' is a grammarians' descriptive label ('double gamma', from the shape); the Greeks who actually used the letter called it ϝαῦ, [wâu̯], which is both the letter's value and a far better teaching object. Modern Greek has no [w] and cannot say it; if the site ever wants that name, Daniel 'wow' gives a near-exact [wau̯] and Luca 'uau' gives it in the Italian voice. I have produced the displayed name as instructed. Accent is stress, not pitch.

25.why: A real Italian word (cup, trophy), [ˈkɔppa], and a near-exact match for the whole syllable shape: an unaspirated [k] — koppa is a k, not a chi — a genuinely held geminate [pː] for the ππ, and a pure unreduced final [a]. Exactly parallel to 'cappa' for Kappa, which is what the two Greek names are to each other. The c-spelling removes any letter-to-sound doubt.
25.compromise: Two things. (1) The ο comes out open, [ɔ], which matches the site's own 'as in German Gott' gloss but not Allen's close-mid [o] — and therefore not the vowel used at Omicron, which follows Allen. That inconsistency is real and is the price of the geminate: Spanish would give the close [o] but has no geminates, and the doubled consonant is the more audible feature. (2) The letter's own value is not in its name. Koppa denoted a backed, uvular-ish [q]-like allophone of k before back vowels — that backing is precisely why the letter existed alongside kappa — and no voice here produces it; you will hear a plain kappa, which is in fact what the NAME contains. The letter was obsolete in Attic by the classical period, so its name's accentuation is reconstructed by analogy with κάππα rather than attested. Accent is stress, not pitch.

26.why: Italian keeps [mp] as a voiceless, unaspirated cluster, which is the whole difficulty: this is where the Greek-first strategy inverts on itself, because the μπ digraph that rescues Beta destroys Sampi — Melina reading σαμπί gives [saˈbi], the p voiced and the m absorbed, and there is no Greek spelling for [mp] at all, since μπ is [b] or [mb] in every position by rule. The final grave is the one accent position standard Italian orthography actually uses, so it fires: 'sampì' (0.639 s, 8cce5952…) against 'sampi' (0.748 s, d6d0479b…), a 110 ms difference that is a genuine stress shift onto the final syllable, matching oxytone σαμπῖ.
26.compromise: The least secure entry here, and the uncertainty is in the target, not only the recipe. The name is a late and probably folk-etymological coinage ('like a pi'); the letter's archaic name is unknown; its accentuation is an editorial choice (most modern usage says SAM-pi); and its sound value is contested, as the site itself says — 'perhaps ss or ts'. So this voices a conventional modern reading of an uncertain name rather than a reconstruction anyone can vouch for. Mechanically: the final [i] is SHORT, not the long [iː] of σαμπῖ — Italian lengthens stressed vowels in non-final open syllables only, and the accent here in fact shortened the word rather than lengthening it. Ignore any claim that the grave buys length. Accent is stress, not pitch.

modern.note: How a Greek speaker says the letter today — offered so the distance travelled can be heard.

0.why: Modern Greek alpha is a plain open [a] in both syllables; Melina reads the ordinary word directly.
0.compromise: The name itself is unchanged since antiquity, but the modern vowel system has lost phonemic length: ancient ἄλφα had a long final alpha, and modern Greek makes no long/short distinction at all. The ancient pitch accent is likewise gone — Melina delivers a modern stress accent.

1.why: Modern beta is the fricative [v], and eta has merged into [i]; the name is heard as 'VEE-ta'.
1.compromise: This is the clearest sound-change in the alphabet: ancient [b] has spirantised to [v], and the name's ancient long open [ɛː] has raised and merged with iota. The modern spelling is identical to the ancient; only the reading has moved.

2.why: Modern gamma before a back vowel is the voiced velar fricative [ɣ], a soft throaty g, not the hard [g] of antiquity.
2.compromise: Ancient hard [g] has spirantised to [ɣ] (and would be [ʝ] before front vowels). The double mu is orthographic only: modern Greek has degeminated, so Melina says a single [m] — the spelling γάμα is equally current. Length and pitch accent are lost as elsewhere.

3.why: Modern delta is the voiced dental fricative [ð], the th of 'this'.
3.compromise: Ancient [d] has spirantised to [ð]; the ancient plain stop survives in modern Greek only in the digraph ντ. The name and its spelling are otherwise unchanged from the classical form, and the accent is stress rather than pitch.

4.why: Read as spelt: mid front [e], then the cluster [ps], then [i], then [on] — 'E-psee-lon'.
4.compromise: The name is a Byzantine coinage meaning 'bare e', invented to distinguish this letter from the digraph αι once the two had merged in sound. A classical Athenian called the letter simply εἶ. The modern audio therefore names the letter correctly for a modern reader but is anachronistic as a classical name.

5.why: Modern zeta is a simple voiced [z], and eta is [i]: 'ZEE-ta'.
5.compromise: The ancient cluster [zd] (the site's 'wisdom' gloss) simplified to a single [z] already in the Hellenistic period, and the name's [ɛː] has raised to [i]. Two distinct ancient features are absent here — which is precisely the contrast this modern track exists to show.

6.why: Eta is now simply [i]; the name is 'EE-ta'.
6.compromise: The single largest vowel shift in the language: ancient long open [ɛː] raised through [e] to [i] and merged with iota, upsilon and three digraphs (iotacism). The ancient length contrast with epsilon is entirely gone, and in modern audio eta's name is nearly indistinguishable in vowel quality from iota's.

7.why: Modern theta is the voiceless dental fricative [θ], the th of 'thin'.
7.compromise: Ancient theta was an aspirated stop [tʰ] — a t followed by a puff of breath — not a fricative. English speakers who read ancient Greek with 'th' as in 'thin' are unwittingly using the modern value. Eta is again [i] rather than [ɛː].

8.why: The standard modern name begins with the palatal glide [ʝ], written γι-; Melina reads γιώτα as 'YO-ta', stressed on the first syllable.
8.compromise: Spelt γιώτα rather than the older ιώτα so the voice produces the genuine modern [ˈʝota] instead of a spelling-pronounced two-vowel [iˈota]; both spellings are current and the sound is the same, but this one gets it reliably. In antiquity the name was [iˈɔːta], with the initial iota a full vowel and the omega long — modern Greek has neither the length nor the hiatus.

9.why: Greek [k] is unaspirated then and now, and both vowels are plain [a]: 'KA-pa'.
9.compromise: Little has moved here — the modern name preserves the ancient consonant and vowels almost exactly, and Greek still refuses to aspirate initial k. But the double pi is orthographic: modern Greek degeminates, so Melina says a single [p] where a classical speaker held the geminate. Pitch accent is replaced by stress.

10.why: The modern spelling λάμδα gives [ˈlamða]: clear [l], then delta as the fricative [ð].
10.compromise: The ancient name was λάμβδα, pronounced [ˈlambda] with a real [b] and [d]. Modern Greek has both simplified the spelling and spirantised the delta, so the ancient cluster is doubly obscured. The variant λάμβδα is still written but would be read [ˈlamvða] — further from the ancient sound, not closer.

11.why: Upsilon has merged into [i], so the modern name is simply 'mee'.
11.compromise: Ancient μῦ was [myː], with the front rounded vowel and a long circumflex-accented nucleus; modern Greek lost [y] to iotacism, leaving a bare short [i]. Slowed to 140 wpm because a single light syllable in isolation is otherwise clipped almost to nothing.

12.why: As with mu, upsilon is now [i]: the name is 'nee'.
12.compromise: Ancient νῦ was [nyː], long and front-rounded; both the rounding and the length are gone, and the name is now homophonous with English 'knee'. Rate lowered so the one-syllable name is audible.

13.why: Xi still spells the cluster [ks]; the name is a single syllable, 'ksee'.
13.compromise: The consonant value is unchanged — one of the most stable letters — but the ancient name was ξεῖ [kseː], with a long e-vowel since raised to [i]. As a monosyllable the modern name carries no written accent; rate lowered so the initial cluster is not swallowed.

14.why: Read as spelt with stress on the first syllable: 'O-mee-kron', literally 'little o'.
14.compromise: A Byzantine coinage like epsilon: the name means 'small o' and was needed only after omicron and omega had merged in sound, which they have — modern Greek pronounces both as the same [o]. The classical name for the letter was simply οὖ, and the ancient short/long contrast with omega no longer exists.

15.why: Greek initial [p] is unaspirated then and now; the name is a crisp 'pee' with no puff of breath.
15.compromise: The consonant is faithful to antiquity, but the ancient name was πεῖ [peː], with a long close e that iotacism has raised to [i] — so modern 'pi' rhymes with 'see', not with 'say'. The English 'pie' is neither ancient nor modern. Rate lowered for the monosyllable.

16.why: Modern rho is a single alveolar tap [ɾ] or light trill, followed by [o].
16.compromise: Modern Greek normally taps rather than fully trills, where classical rho was a true trill, and the classical initial rough breathing (the breathy [r̥] of ῥῶ) has vanished from both spelling and sound. The omega is now a short [o], not the ancient long open [ɔː]. Rate lowered for the monosyllable.

17.why: Sibilant [s], then gamma as the voiced fricative [ɣ] before the [m].
17.compromise: The [s] is unchanged, but the internal gamma has spirantised: ancient [ˈsiɡma], with a hard g, has become [ˈsiɣma]. Melina may also partly voice the sibilant before the following voiced consonant, as modern Greek regularly does. Pitch accent replaced by stress.

18.why: The modern digraph αυ is [af] finally and before a voiceless consonant, so the name is heard as 'taf'.
18.compromise: A striking change: the ancient diphthong [taʊ] has become consonant-final [taf], because upsilon in diphthongs fricativised to [f]/[v]. The [t] itself is unaspirated in both eras. Anyone expecting English 'tow' or 'taw' is using neither pronunciation. Rate lowered for the monosyllable.

19.why: Upsilon is now [i], so the name is 'EE-psee-lon', stressed on the first syllable.
19.compromise: Doubly displaced from antiquity. The name is a Byzantine coinage — 'bare u', distinguishing the letter from the digraph οι once the two merged — where the classical name was simply ῦ; and the letter's own sound, the front rounded [y] of French 'lune', is entirely lost, merged into [i]. The modern audio gives no hint of what upsilon once was.

20.why: Modern phi is the labiodental fricative [f]; the name is 'fee'.
20.compromise: Ancient phi was aspirated [pʰ] — a p with a puff of breath — not [f]; the fricative is a later development, though it gave us the transliteration 'ph' in 'philosophy'. The ancient name φεῖ also had a long e, now raised to [i]. Rate lowered for the monosyllable.

21.why: Before a front vowel modern chi is the palatal fricative [ç], the sound of German 'ich'; the name is like English 'hee' with audible friction.
21.compromise: Ancient chi was aspirated [kʰ], a k plus breath, not a fricative at all. The modern reflex is [x] before back vowels and [ç] before front ones — and because the name's vowel is [i], the audio gives the palatal allophone rather than the throatier [x] most readers expect. The ancient name χεῖ had a long e. Rate lowered for the monosyllable.

22.why: Psi still spells the cluster [ps], fully pronounced word-initially in Greek — 'psee', not 'see'.
22.compromise: The cluster is unchanged since antiquity — Greek keeps the initial [ps] that English drops in 'psychology' — but the ancient name ψεῖ had a long close e now raised to [i]. So the consonant is a good witness to the ancient letter and the vowel is not. Rate lowered so the cluster is not swallowed.

23.why: Stress falls on the middle syllable and the gamma is the voiced fricative [ɣ]: 'o-MEH-gha'.
23.compromise: A Byzantine coinage meaning 'big o', coined once omega and omicron sounded alike — as they now do, both plain [o]. The classical name was simply ὦ, a single long [ɔː], and the letter's defining feature, its length, no longer exists in the language. Note too that the common English 'OH-mega', stressed on the first syllable, is wrong in both ancient and modern Greek.

24.why: Read as an ordinary modern Greek word: [ð] for delta, [ɣ] for gamma — 'THEE-gha-ma', the 'double gamma', named for its shape.
24.compromise: An antiquarian name, not a living pronunciation: digamma had dropped out of the Attic alphabet before the classical period, and modern Greek has no sound for it — what Melina gives is a modern reading of a scholarly label, not the letter in use. Its value was [w], which modern Greek does not possess at all. Both consonants of the name have themselves spirantised, and the double mu is degeminated.

25.why: Read as spelt with unaspirated [k] and a single [p]: 'KO-pa'.
25.compromise: Antiquarian like digamma: koppa fell out of alphabetic use in the archaic period and survived only as the numeral 90, so it has no modern spoken value — the name is a label, not a living letter. The double pi is orthographic and degeminated in Melina's reading. Some sources accent the name κοππά; the first-syllable stress used here is the commoner convention.

26.why: Stress on the final syllable, and the digraph μπ is read [b] (or prenasalised [mb]) as modern Greek requires: 'sa-BEE'.
26.compromise: The most conjectural of the three archaics. The letter's ancient value is genuinely uncertain — perhaps [ss] or [ts] — and 'sampi' is a late, probably medieval coinage said to mean 'like pi'; no ancient Greek called it that. The modern reading is an antiquarian label pronounced by modern rules, with no claim on the letter's real sound. Melina may render μπ as prenasalised [mb] rather than plain [b]; both are current.
